title: The Cell and the Cloister: from the Jura to the Voyage d'Orient to the Sea at Roquebrune
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: La Chaux-de-Fonds, the birth on the Rue de la Serre
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: A son is born to a family of watch-engravers in the Jura town of La Chaux-de-Fonds, a place laid out on a grid after a fire and given over entirely to the making of small precise things. They name him Charles-Edouard Jeanneret-Gris. His father decorates watch cases; his mother teaches piano. The winters are long, the streets run straight, and the trade practised in every house on the street is the fitting of tiny parts into a mechanism that has to keep time. He will spend sixty years enlarging that trade until its object is a city.
suggested_refs: The engravers' quarter of La Chaux-de-Fonds, rebuilt on a grid after the fire of 1794

stops.name: La Chaux-de-Fonds, the Ecole d'Art and Charles L'Eplattenier
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year, 1902; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: At fifteen he enters the municipal art school to learn engraving and the decoration of watch cases, the family trade taught as a discipline. Three years later the painter Charles L'Eplattenier takes him into the higher course of decoration and tells him he is to be an architect. He does not want to be one. He accepts the verdict, in his own later account, the way an apprentice accepts a master's judgement about the grain of a material, and he never afterwards describes the choice as his own.
stops.quote: I had a horror of architecture and architects... I was sixteen, I accepted the verdict and I obeyed. I moved into architecture.
stops.quote_source: Le Corbusier on choosing his career, English translation carried in the Wikipedia article on Le Corbusier, footnote 21
suggested_refs: The Ecole d'Art of La Chaux-de-Fonds and L'Eplattenier's cours superieur de decoration

stops.name: La Chaux-de-Fonds, the Villa Fallet
stops.date_confidence: designed 1905; Wikipedia's Villa Fallet article gives completion 1906, other sources 1907. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: At eighteen, still a student, he designs a house for an engraver who sits on the school's board, and builds it with the local contractor Rene Chapallaz on the slope of Pouillerel above the town. Chalet roofs, carved gables, pine and fir cut into geometric ornament: the vocabulary is the Jura's own, taught by L'Eplattenier as a regional style. Nothing in it forecasts the white boxes. What it establishes is that the boy can get a building out of the ground, and the fee sends him to Italy.
suggested_refs: Villa Fallet, 1 Chemin de Pouillerel, his first executed building

stops.name: Florence, the Charterhouse of Ema
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1907; day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: His first journey outside Switzerland ends on a hill south of Florence at the Carthusian charterhouse of Galluzzo. Each monk holds a private cell with its own walled garden; all the cells open onto a shared cloister; the community prays in common and sleeps alone. He walks through it and reads the arrangement as a diagram rather than as a rule of life. Forty-six years later he will build it again in concrete for Dominicans at Eveux, and he will say plainly that this is where he first saw it.
suggested_refs: The Certosa del Galluzzo (Charterhouse of Ema), south of Florence

stops.name: Vienna, the winter after Italy
stops.date_confidence: wintered 1907 into 1908; exact months not fixed by any source consulted, defaulted to December
stops.campa: From Italy he travels on through Budapest to Vienna and stays the winter. The city is at the height of the Secession, and he meets Gustav Klimt among the painters and craftsmen who are arguing ornament into a moral question. Jeanneret is twenty and carries a portfolio of carved gables from a Swiss chalet. He is about to spend a decade unlearning them. He leaves in the spring for Paris, without a commission, without money, and without any settled idea of what a modern building should look like.
suggested_refs: The Vienna Secession milieu of 1907-1908, and Klimt's studio

stops.name: Paris, the office of Auguste Perret
stops.date_confidence: roughly fourteen months across 1908-1910; start month not fixed, defaulted to March 1908
stops.campa: He works some fourteen months for Auguste Perret, whose apartment house at 25bis rue Franklin is the first building in Paris to show its reinforced-concrete frame and admit that the frame is what holds it up. Perret pays him almost nothing and argues with him constantly. Jeanneret learns the material: a skeleton of columns and slabs frees the wall from bearing weight, and a wall that bears no weight may be opened anywhere. Gabriele d'Annunzio is holding court in the salons of the same city those years; the two men share the streets and nothing else.
suggested_refs: 25bis rue Franklin, Paris, Perret's reinforced-concrete apartment building and office

stops.name: Berlin, the office of Peter Behrens
stops.date_confidence: October 1910 to March 1911, attested to the months
stops.campa: Five months in Peter Behrens's Berlin office, in the shadow of the AEG turbine hall, a factory built with the mass and the dignity of a temple. Ludwig Mies van der Rohe is at the next drawing board. Behrens is designing everything the electrical company makes, from kettles to letterheads to the buildings, and Jeanneret sees for the first time an architect operating at the scale of an industry. He dislikes the man and says so for the rest of his life, while conceding the lesson.
stops.quote: You can see, that Auguste Perret left more in me than Peter Behrens.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Auguste Perret, July 1916, English translation carried in the Wikipedia article on Le Corbusier, footnote 33
suggested_refs: The AEG Turbine Factory, Huttenstrasse, Berlin, built by Behrens 1909

segments.name: The Voyage d'Orient: East by the Danube

stops.name: Prague, the Old Town Square
stops.date_confidence: May 1911, from the itinerary reconstruction of the Voyage d'Orient; not a dated letter
stops.campa: In May he sets out east with August Klipstein, a German art-history student, on a journey that will run five months and reach Athens by way of the Danube. Prague is the first stop after Berlin and Dresden. He draws the Gothic silhouette of the square, the tower and the clock and the crowd, and begins the practice that will define the whole trip: he does not photograph, he draws, because a drawing takes long enough that the eye is forced to understand what the hand is copying.
suggested_refs: The eighty sketchbooks of the 1911 Voyage d'Orient, Fondation Le Corbusier
sources: Elke Krasny, account of Le Corbusier's Voyage d'Orient
Le Corbusier, Journey to the East (written 1911, published 1966)

stops.name: Budapest, the Danube quays
stops.date_confidence: May 1911, from the itinerary reconstruction; day unknown
stops.campa: The route follows the river. In Budapest he notes the traffic on the water and the two cities on their two banks, the Habsburg fabric on one side and something older and further east showing through on the other. His letters home from this leg record restlessness rather than sightseeing. He is travelling toward something he cannot yet name, on a budget that requires third-class carriages and cheap rooms, and the sketchbooks are filling faster than the letters.
suggested_refs: The Danube quays of Pest and the Buda hill, drawn in May 1911
sources: Elke Krasny, account of Le Corbusier's Voyage d'Orient

stops.name: Belgrade, Kalemegdan above the confluence
stops.date_confidence: June 1911, from the itinerary reconstruction; day unknown
stops.campa: At the fortress where the Sava enters the Danube he draws the Serbian capital as a frontier town, its Ottoman walls and its Habsburg guns and its recent wars all legible from one parapet. The Balkan states are between one war and the next; within two years the armies will be moving through here again. He looks at the peasant houses as hard as at the fortifications, and writes down what whitewash and a plain wall and a well-placed window can do without an architect.
suggested_refs: Kalemegdan fortress, Belgrade, above the Sava-Danube confluence
sources: Elke Krasny, account of Le Corbusier's Voyage d'Orient

stops.name: Istanbul, Hagia Sophia
stops.date_confidence: the Constantinople stay runs roughly six weeks across June and July 1911; day unknown
stops.campa: He and Klipstein stay roughly six weeks in Constantinople, and he returns again and again to Justinian's church: the dome floating on its pendentives, the buttresses that hold it up, the light entering at the base of the vault so that the mass appears to rest on nothing. He calls it one of the buildings that overturns his sense of what architecture is. Nine years later Gurdjieff will open his institute in Pera, a mile from where the two students are sleeping; nothing connects them but the pavement.
suggested_refs: Hagia Sophia, drawn repeatedly in the 1911 sketchbooks
sources: Le Corbusier, Journey to the East

stops.name: Istanbul, the Suleymaniye
stops.date_confidence: July 1911, within the six-week Constantinople stay; day unknown
stops.campa: He climbs to Sinan's courtyard above the Golden Horn to study how one architect stacked domes and placed minarets so that the whole mass reads correctly from three miles away across water. It is a lesson in silhouette, and it is the lesson he will invoke against his own century when he argues that a tower is not yet tall enough. He also fills pages with the wooden houses of the Turkish street, the cheapest building in the city, drawn with the same attention as the mosque.
suggested_refs: The Suleymaniye Mosque of Mimar Sinan, and the timber houses of old Stamboul
sources: Le Corbusier, Journey to the East

segments.name: The Holy Mountain and the Ruins

stops.name: Mount Athos, the Great Lavra
stops.date_confidence: August 1911, from the itinerary reconstruction; day unknown
stops.campa: They sail down the monastic peninsula and land at the oldest house on it, founded in the tenth century by Athanasius. No woman has set foot on this ground in nine hundred years. He walks the cells and the refectory and the courtyards and writes about the monks the way he wrote about the Charterhouse of Ema four years earlier: not as a believer but as a surveyor of a working machine for common life. Athos and Ema are the two halves of a single idea he will carry to the end.
suggested_refs: The Great Lavra, founded 963 by Athanasius the Athonite, oldest monastery of Mount Athos
sources: Le Corbusier, Journey to the East

stops.name: Mount Athos, Simonopetra
stops.date_confidence: August 1911, from the itinerary reconstruction; day unknown
stops.campa: Simonopetra stands on a rock above the sea, seven storeys of monastery with wooden balconies hung out over a sheer drop, so that the site performs the work the walls cannot. He draws it repeatedly and calls it in his letters the most extraordinary thing on the mountain. The image stays with him. Half a century later he will set a monastery on a slope at Eveux, hang the cells over the fall of the ground on legs of unequal length, and let the terrain carry the drama.
suggested_refs: Simonopetra monastery on its cliff, Mount Athos
sources: Le Corbusier, Journey to the East

stops.name: Athens, the Parthenon
stops.date_confidence: September 1911, weeks in Athens; day unknown
stops.campa: He stays weeks in Athens and climbs the rock at dawn to draw in the changing light. What he takes from the Parthenon is not the orders but the corrections: the columns lean inward, the stylobate curves, no line in the building is actually straight, and the whole apparatus of adjustment exists so that the eye will read the thing as perfect. He writes that the temple taught him more than any book. Isadora Duncan had built her clan a temple on the hill below eight years earlier, on the same conviction.
suggested_refs: The Parthenon studies of the 1911 sketchbooks, reprinted in Vers une architecture
sources: Le Corbusier, Journey to the East

stops.name: Pompeii, the atrium houses
stops.date_confidence: October 1911, on the Italian return leg; day unknown
stops.campa: The return runs through Italy. In the excavated streets he measures the atrium houses: a blank wall to the road, a court open to the sky at the centre, the rooms turned inward on the light of that court. The plan admits nothing of the street and everything of the sun. He copies them into the sketchbooks with the dimensions written in, and he will go on drawing versions of the same arrangement, in concrete and lifted on columns, for the rest of his working life.
suggested_refs: The atrium houses of Pompeii, measured in the 1911 sketchbooks
sources: Le Corbusier, Journey to the East

stops.name: Rome, the Pantheon
stops.date_confidence: October into November 1911; day unknown
stops.campa: In Rome he measures the drum and the oculus and the single unbroken hemisphere above them, a building whose entire argument is one hole in one dome and the disc of sunlight that travels the wall all day. Twelve years later he will print it in his manifesto beside photographs of an ocean liner and a motor car and claim all three for one lineage: masses assembled so that light does the explaining. He is twenty-four and has not yet built anything he will later admit to.
stops.quote: Architecture is the masterly, correct and magnificent play of masses brought together in light.
stops.quote_source: Vers une architecture (1923), trans. Frederick Etchells, Towards a New Architecture (1927)
suggested_refs: The Pantheon, Rome, and its treatment in Vers une architecture
sources: Le Corbusier, Journey to the East

stops.name: La Chaux-de-Fonds, the return with eighty sketchbooks
stops.date_confidence: November 1911; day unknown
stops.campa: He comes home to his parents' town in November after five months on the road, carrying some eighty sketchbooks and a vocabulary that is now essentially fixed: the cell and the cloister, the whitewashed wall, the plan turned inward on a court, the dome resting on light, the correction that makes a straight line look straight. He will not build in that vocabulary for another decade. First he has to design houses for watchmakers, study concrete with an engineer, and lose the Jura.
suggested_refs: The Voyage d'Orient sketchbooks, deposited with the Fondation Le Corbusier
sources: Le Corbusier, Journey to the East

segments.name: Purism and the Rue de Sevres

stops.name: La Chaux-de-Fonds, the Villa Schwob
stops.date_confidence: Wikipedia's Le Corbusier article dates the commission to August 1916; its Villa Schwob article dates commission 1912 and completion 1917. Conflict unresolved.
stops.campa: For a watch manufacturer he builds the house the town calls the Villa Turque: reinforced concrete, a double-height living hall, an apsidal end, a blank wall to the street and a great sheet of glass to the garden. The client and the architect quarrel about money and about everything else. It is the last building he puts up in the Jura and the first in which the free facade is visible rather than argued. The following year he leaves Switzerland for Paris and never lives there again.
stops.quote: Whether you like it or not, my presence is inscribed in every corner of your house.
stops.quote_source: Reported reply to the client Anatole Schwob, English translation carried in the Wikipedia article on Le Corbusier, footnote 34
suggested_refs: Villa Schwob (Villa Turque), rue du Doubs, La Chaux-de-Fonds

stops.name: Paris, the name taken in L'Esprit Nouveau
stops.date_confidence: the first issue of L'Esprit Nouveau appears in autumn 1920; month taken as October, day unknown
stops.campa: With the painter Amedee Ozenfant, met in 1918, he has published Apres le Cubisme and declared Purism: no decoration, no distortion, objects reduced to the forms a machine would give them. Now the two found a review, and for the pieces on architecture Jeanneret signs a name adapted from a maternal ancestor called Lecorbesier. The painter keeps his own name. The architect invents one, in the third person, and answers to it for the next forty-five years.
stops.quote_source: Vers une architecture (1923), trans. Frederick Etchells, Towards a New Architecture (1927)
suggested_refs: L'Esprit Nouveau, first issue, 1920, and the Purist manifesto Apres le Cubisme (1918)

stops.name: Paris, the atelier at 35 rue de Sevres
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1922; month unknown, defaulted. The gathered pool wrongly dated the partnership from 1917.
stops.campa: He and his cousin Pierre Jeanneret take a corridor in a former Jesuit convent at 35 rue de Sevres and open a studio in it. The room is bad, long and narrow and poorly lit, and nearly every project of the next four decades is drawn there, largely by unpaid assistants from a dozen countries. Marcel Proust dies in Paris that same year, in a cork-lined room across the river, having spent it recovering the past. The men in the corridor are drawing a city that keeps none of it.
suggested_refs: The atelier at 35 rue de Sevres, Paris, in use from 1922 to 1965

stops.name: Paris, Vers une architecture
stops.date_confidence: published 1923; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The articles from the review are gathered into a book, and the book changes European building more than anything he has yet raised. It sets photographs of grain silos and biplanes and the liner Aquitania against the Parthenon and asks the reader to see one argument running through all of them. It says that the styles are a lie and that a house is a machine for living in, and the second half of that sentence is quoted for a century by people who never read the first.
stops.quote: A house is a machine for living in.
stops.quote_source: Vers une architecture (1923), trans. Frederick Etchells, Towards a New Architecture (1927), rendering 'Une maison est une machine-a-habiter'
suggested_refs: Vers une architecture, Cres, 1923; Etchells translation, London, 1927
sources: Frederick Etchells, Towards a New Architecture (1927), full text

stops.name: Paris, the Pavillon de l'Esprit Nouveau and the Plan Voisin
stops.date_confidence: the exhibition runs through 1925; month of the pavilion's opening not fixed here, defaulted
stops.campa: At the international exhibition of decorative arts he builds a pavilion with no decorative art inside it: a single standard apartment cell furnished with laboratory glassware, bentwood chairs and factory cabinets. On its wall he hangs the Plan Voisin, a proposal to flatten several hundred acres of central Paris north of the Seine and stand eighteen cruciform towers in a park. The city ignores it. The drawing travels the world and gets built, in fragments, by cities that never asked him.
stops.quote: It is a question of building which is at the root of the social unrest of to-day: architecture or revolution.
stops.quote_source: Vers une architecture (1923), trans. Frederick Etchells, Towards a New Architecture (1927), from the final chapter 'Architecture or Revolution'. It is not the book's closing line.
suggested_refs: The Pavillon de l'Esprit Nouveau and the Plan Voisin panels, Exposition des Arts Decoratifs, Paris 1925

stops.name: Pessac, the Cite Fruges
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1926; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Outside Bordeaux the sugar industrialist Henry Fruges gives him a field and tells him to experiment. He builds worker housing in raw cubic blocks, standardized, flat-roofed, painted in slabs of colour so the volumes read against each other from a distance. The residents move in, put pitched roofs on some of the houses, glaze the terraces and divide the open plans with walls. He treats the alterations as a failure of the client rather than a failure of the design.
stops.quote: Modern life demands, and is waiting for, a new kind of plan, both for the house and the city.
stops.quote_source: Vers une architecture (1923), trans. Frederick Etchells, Towards a New Architecture (1927)
suggested_refs: Cite Fruges, Pessac, and the photographic record of the residents' modifications

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Weissenhof houses
stops.date_confidence: the estate opens in 1927; month of his houses' completion not fixed here, defaulted
stops.campa: The German Werkbund clears a hillside above Stuttgart and invites the leading modernists of Europe to build on it, with Mies van der Rohe directing. Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret contribute three houses, numbers thirteen to fifteen, and use them to state the five points in public for the first time: the columns, the roof garden, the free plan, the ribbon window, the free facade. Half a million people come to look. The German right calls the estate an Arab village.
stops.quote: Our own epoch is determining, day by day, its own style.
stops.quote_source: Vers une architecture (1923), trans. Frederick Etchells, Towards a New Architecture (1927). The widely circulated wording 'Our epoch determines each day its style' belongs to a different translation, not to Etchells.
suggested_refs: Weissenhofsiedlung houses 13-15 by Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret, Stuttgart 1927

stops.name: La Sarraz, the founding of CIAM
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: In a medieval castle in the Vaud, above Lake Leman, architects from several countries meet at the invitation of Helene de Mandrot and constitute the Congres Internationaux d'Architecture Moderne. Le Corbusier presides. The declaration they sign turns modern architecture from a taste into a programme: standardization, rationalized production, and the planning of cities treated as a technical matter for specialists. For thirty years CIAM is the instrument through which his ideas reach governments.
suggested_refs: The Chateau de la Sarraz and the CIAM declaration of 28 June 1928

stops.name: Poissy, the Villa Savoye
stops.date_confidence: designed and built 1928-1931; month of commencement not fixed here, defaulted
stops.campa: On a meadow above the Seine he builds the clearest statement of the five points: a white box on thin columns, a ramp turning up through the middle of it, a strip window running the full width of every face, a garden on the roof and a curved screen wall set around it against the wind. It is a summer house for a family in insurance. It leaks from the first winter, a damp room makes the son ill, and the Savoyes threaten to sue. The house outlives the quarrel and becomes the most reproduced dwelling of the century.
suggested_refs: Villa Savoye, Poissy, and the Savoye family's correspondence about the roof

stops.name: Moscow, the Tsentrosoyuz
stops.date_confidence: begun 1928 or 1929; Wikipedia's Le Corbusier article says completed 1932, its Tsentrosoyuz article 1933, much of the literature 1936. Unresolved.
stops.campa: Soviet planners hand him the headquarters of the state consumers' cooperative on Myasnitskaya Street: glass curtain walls, ramps in place of staircases for four thousand clerks, and a system of heated and cooled air he calls respiration exacte. He travels repeatedly to Moscow while it goes up, and it takes years longer than promised. When he enters the larger competition for the Palace of the Soviets in 1932 the commission goes to a Stalinist wedding cake, and the Soviet door shuts behind him.
suggested_refs: The Tsentrosoyuz building, 39 Myasnitskaya Street, Moscow

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the lectures that become Precisions
stops.date_confidence: the South American tour runs through the second half of 1929; month approximate, day unknown
stops.campa: He crosses the Atlantic for the first time and gives a series of lectures in Buenos Aires, drawing in coloured chalk on great sheets of paper while he speaks, then flies over the delta and the brown river and returns with a plan to build the city a new business quarter on a platform out in the water. The lectures are printed the following year as Precisions. Emin Arslan, the exiled Ottoman consul turned Buenos Aires editor, has been a fixture of the same press world for nineteen years by then.
suggested_refs: Precisions sur un etat present de l'architecture et de l'urbanisme (1930), the transcript of the Buenos Aires lectures

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo
stops.date_confidence: 1929; the Buenos Aires tour is attested, the Ocampo hospitality is tradition and is unattested in any file or source checked here
stops.campa: Victoria Ocampo's house at San Isidro is the hinge of the circuit that brings European visitors to the Plate, and the tradition holds that he stays there and lectures under her patronage. Hermann Keyserling had been received at the same table in July of the same year. Two Januaries later Jorge Luis Borges will sit in these rooms at the founding of Sur. No document consulted names Le Corbusier among her guests, and the connection rests on tradition alone.
suggested_refs: Villa Ocampo, San Isidro, and the guest lists of the 1929 lecture season

stops.name: Algiers, the Plan Obus
stops.date_confidence: the Algiers proposals run 1931-1942; month of the first scheme not fixed here, defaulted
stops.campa: From the heights of Fort l'Empereur he looks down on colonial Algiers and proposes to run one continuous residential viaduct along the bay, fourteen storeys of housing carried beneath an elevated motorway, the whole coast rebuilt as a single object. He comes back to the city with variants for eleven years. The municipality builds none of it. Nothing in Algiers changes because of him, and nothing in his thinking changes because of Algiers.
stops.quote: The Despot is not a man. It is the Plan. The correct, realistic, exact plan.
suggested_refs: The Plan Obus drawings for Algiers, 1931-1942, Fondation Le Corbusier

stops.name: New York, the skyscrapers judged too small
stops.date_confidence: the first American tour falls in 1935; month approximate, day unknown
stops.campa: He lands in the United States for the first time, is met by reporters at the pier, and tells them the skyscrapers of Manhattan are much too small. He means it technically: too close together, too many of them, too little light and open ground between them, a good idea executed without a plan. The papers print it as an insult and he spends two months touring the country explaining himself. The book he writes afterward gives the city both halves of his verdict at once.
stops.quote: A hundred times I have thought: New York is a catastrophe, and fifty times: it is a beautiful catastrophe.
stops.quote_source: When the Cathedrals Were White (1947), his account of the 1935 tour of the United States
suggested_refs: Quand les cathedrales etaient blanches (1937), written after the 1935 American tour
sources: Le Corbusier, When the Cathedrals Were White

segments.name: The Occupation and the Concrete Years

stops.name: Ozon, the Pyrenean retreat
stops.date_confidence: at Ozon from 1940 to 1942; month of arrival not fixed here, defaulted
stops.campa: With Paris occupied he withdraws to a village in the Hautes-Pyrenees and stays more than a year, largely idle, painting and writing and sending unanswered letters to anyone who might commission a city. He is fifty-three and has built almost nothing at scale: the Radiant City exists as a book, the Plan Voisin as a drawing. From the village he begins writing toward Vichy, where a government that consults nobody is proposing to rebuild France.
suggested_refs: Ozon, Hautes-Pyrenees, and the correspondence of the 1940-1942 retreat

stops.name: Vichy, Ascoral and the Carrel foundation
stops.date_confidence: Ascoral founded 1943; the resignation from the Carrel foundation is attested to 20 April 1944. Month of the founding unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He spends months at Vichy pressing his urbanism on the new regime and obtains nothing built. He founds Ascoral to plan the reconstruction and takes a place in the eugenics foundation of Alexis Carrel, from which he resigns on the twentieth of April 1944. After the Liberation the episode is set aside for seventy years; in 2015 two books put the interwar sympathies and the Vichy months back on the table. What is attested is the date of the resignation. What is contested is everything before it.
suggested_refs: Xavier de Jarcy, Le Corbusier, un fascisme francais (2015); Francois Chaslin, Un Corbusier (2015)

stops.name: New York, the United Nations design board
stops.date_confidence: the design board sits in 1947; construction runs to 1952. Month unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He sits on the international board of design for the headquarters on the East River and contributes the scheme for the Secretariat slab, the tall thin block with two blank ends and two glass faces. Execution passes to Wallace Harrison and the presentation to Oscar Niemeyer, whose scheme is merged with his own. He spends years afterward asserting that the building is his, and receives no official credit for it. The tower goes up as a committee's work and reads, from the river, as his.
suggested_refs: The United Nations Headquarters board of design, 1947, and the Secretariat scheme 23A

stops.name: Marseille, the Unite d'Habitation
stops.date_confidence: built 1947-1952; month of commencement not fixed here, defaulted
stops.campa: On the boulevard Michelet the French state finally gives him the commission he has been drawing since 1922: 337 apartments in one slab on massive tapered columns, flats interlocked in section, interior streets in place of corridors, a shopping street on the seventh floor, and a roof carrying a nursery school, a gymnasium and a running track above the sea. The concrete is left rough from the shuttering because the contractors cannot do better, and he keeps it that way and gives the surface a name.
stops.quote: My own duty and my aim is to try and raise people out of their misery, away from catastrophe; to provide them with happiness, with a contented existence, with harmony. My own goal is to establish or re-establish harmony between people and their environment.
stops.quote_source: Quoted in Jean Jenger, Le Corbusier: Architect, Painter, Poet (1996), as reproduced on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Unite d'Habitation, 280 boulevard Michelet, Marseille; the second Unite at Reze was completed in 1955

stops.name: Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, Le Cabanon
stops.date_confidence: built 1952; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: On a rock above the Mediterranean, on ground just east of Eileen Gray's villa E-1027, he builds himself a hut of 3.66 metres square in logs, proportioned throughout to the Modulor, his measuring system derived from a man of six feet with one arm raised. It holds a bed, a table, a stool and a washbasin, and it has no kitchen; he eats next door at the restaurant. He and Yvonne summer here every year until she dies in 1957, and afterward he comes alone.
suggested_refs: Le Cabanon at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, and the Modulor scale of 1948

stops.name: Ronchamp, Notre-Dame du Haut
stops.date_confidence: designed from 1950, completed 1955; month of the commission unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: For a hilltop pilgrimage site in the Vosges he abandons the machine vocabulary altogether. The walls curve and thicken, the roof rises at one corner like an upturned hull and floats clear of the wall on a slot of daylight, and the south wall is pierced by deep splayed openings of coloured glass set as if scattered. Modernists who had followed him for thirty years accuse him of betrayal. He answers that the site asked for it. It becomes a place people walk uphill to reach.
suggested_refs: Chapelle Notre-Dame-du-Haut, Ronchamp, consecrated 1955

stops.name: Eveux, Sainte Marie de La Tourette
stops.date_confidence: design begun May 1953; construction 1956-1960
stops.campa: Dominican friars ask him for a monastery on a hillside outside Lyon and he gives them the Charterhouse of Ema in raw concrete: a hundred individual cells stacked in two floors around the top of a square, each with its narrow balcony, the whole hung over the fall of the ground on legs of unequal length. Below the cells lie the shared rooms, the cloister and a windowless church lit through tubes he calls light cannons. He first saw the arrangement at Galluzzo in 1907, and he says so.
suggested_refs: Couvent Sainte-Marie de La Tourette, Eveux-sur-l'Arbresle

stops.name: Chandigarh, the Capitol Complex begun
stops.date_confidence: recruited between November and December 1950; first visit February 1951. Day unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: Punjab has lost Lahore to the partition and needs a capital. The American planner engaged first is replaced, and at the end of 1950 Le Corbusier is recruited to head a team of four. He arrives in February 1951, lays a grid of numbered sectors on the plain below the Himalayan foothills, and reserves the head of the city for a group of government buildings standing far apart from one another across an open esplanade. He will return to India almost every year he has left.
stops.quote: The city of Chandigarh is planned to human scale.
suggested_refs: The Chandigarh masterplan of 1951 and the sector grid

stops.name: Ahmedabad, the Mill Owners' Association
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1954; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The textile owners of Ahmedabad commission a headquarters on the bank of the Sabarmati, and he turns the whole west face into a grid of deep concrete fins set at an angle to the sun, a brise-soleil that shades the rooms and admits the river wind. In the same city he builds villas for the Sarabhai and the Shodhan families. The device invented here for Gujarati heat travels back to Europe with him and is applied afterward to buildings in climates that never needed it.
suggested_refs: Mill Owners' Association Building, Ashram Road, Ahmedabad; Villa Sarabhai and Villa Shodhan

stops.name: Chandigarh, the Palace of Assembly completed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1962; month unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The legislature is finished eleven years after he first saw the site: a great portico with an upturned lip, a forest of columns within, and over the assembly chamber a hyperbolic shell in the form of a cooling tower, a shape he had sketched at a thermal power station and kept. The High Court had opened in March 1955 and the Secretariat stands along the same esplanade. He forbids personal statues in the city he plans, and the ban outlasts him.
stops.quote: The age of personal statues is gone.
suggested_refs: The Palace of Assembly, Capitol Complex, Chandigarh; the Edict of Chandigarh, 1959

stops.name: Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, the last swim
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He is seventy-seven and has had a heart attack, and the doctors have told him not to swim. On the morning of the twenty-seventh of August he goes down from the cabin to the water below the rocks and swims out, as he has every summer for thirteen years, and does not come back. Bathers bring him ashore dead. The tradition on this coast says he chose it, that he meant to die in the sea he had built his last house above. No document from that morning says anything of the kind.
stops.quote: Space and light and order. Those are the things that men need just as much as they need bread or a place to sleep.
stops.quote_source: Widely attributed by way of his New York Times obituary, 28 August 1965; the wording circulates only in this posthumous English form and is not traced to any work in his own hand
suggested_refs: The shore below Le Cabanon at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, 27 August 1965

stops.name: Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, the tomb of his own design
stops.date_confidence: burial September 1965; day not fixed by any source consulted, defaulted
stops.campa: He is buried in the hillside cemetery above the old village, in the plot he had made in 1957 when Yvonne died: a low concrete slab and a small coloured cylinder, proportioned like everything else he built, with the sea in view below it. That he designed it himself is what the biographers say and what the object itself argues; no document examined for this journey proves it. It is the last structure in a life spent drawing the place where he would stand.
suggested_refs: The Jeanneret tomb, cimetiere de Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, built 1957
sources: Nicholas Fox Weber, Le Corbusier: A Life (2008), reported at second hand

stops.name: Istanbul, the seventeen works inscribed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: The World Heritage Committee, sitting for its fortieth session in the city where the twenty-three-year-old Jeanneret spent six weeks drawing Hagia Sophia, inscribes seventeen of his buildings across seven countries as one transnational site: France, Switzerland, Germany, Belgium, Argentina, India and Japan. The chapel at Ronchamp, the slab at Marseille, the Capitol at Chandigarh, the cabin at Roquebrune and the Curutchet house at La Plata are all of them on the list.
suggested_refs: 'The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Modern Movement', inscribed 17 July 2016
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier'
